items.prompt: Why does a seedling bend towards the light?

options.label: Its shaded side grows longer than the lit side
options.feedback: Uneven growth is what bends a stem that cannot move.

options.label: Its lit side grows longer
options.feedback: That would bend it the other way, away from the light.

options.label: The light pulls the tip towards itself
options.feedback: Light carries no pull a stem could feel. The bending is done by the plant.

options.label: The stem shrinks on the dark side
options.feedback: Nothing shrinks. A stem bends by adding length on one side, not by losing it on the other.

items.ok_line: A plant turns by growing crooked.
items.ko_line: A bend means one side got longer. Work out which side that has to be.
items.exp_text: A stem has no muscle and nothing that can pull, so the only way it can point somewhere new is to build more of itself on one side. Cells on the shaded flank stretch longer than those facing the light, and the whole stem arches over towards the bright side.

items.prompt: What gathers on the dark side of a stem and makes its cells stretch?

options.label: Water drawn up from the roots
options.feedback: Water reaches both sides equally. It fills the cells but does not decide which ones lengthen.

options.label: A growth substance made in the tip
options.feedback: It is made at the tip, slides to whichever side is darker, and tells those cells to stretch.

options.label: Extra chlorophyll
options.feedback: Chlorophyll is built where light falls, so there is less of it on the dark side, not more.

options.label: Sugar sent down from the leaves
options.feedback: Sugar feeds the whole stem. It is the fuel for growth, not the signal that aims it.

items.ok_line: A messenger that pools in the shade.
items.ko_line: Something has to tell one side to grow and the other not to. Ask what carries that order.
items.exp_title: A messenger that avoids the light
items.exp_text: The very tip of a shoot makes a growth substance and sends it downwards. When light falls on one flank, the substance drifts across to the shaded flank instead. Wherever it collects, the cell walls loosen and the cells lengthen — so the dark side builds more stem, and the shoot leans into the light.

items.prompt: What does a root do when light reaches it?

options.label: It grows towards the light
options.feedback: That would drag the root out of the soil, away from the water it exists to find.

options.label: It stops growing altogether
options.feedback: A root exposed to light keeps growing. It simply changes direction.

options.label: It turns away from it
options.feedback: The opposite response to a shoot, and for the opposite reason.

options.label: It grows faster
options.feedback: Light gives a root nothing. It has no chlorophyll and cannot use it.

items.ok_line: Shoots seek light, roots flee it.
items.ko_line: Ask what a root is looking for. It is not the same thing as a leaf.
items.exp_text: A shoot's business is light, so it grows towards it. A root's business is water and anchorage, both of which lie downwards in the dark. The same kind of uneven growth serves both, simply pointed the other way: where light touches a root, the lit side lengthens and the tip swings back into the soil.

items.prompt: Which way does a young sunflower's head face at sunrise?

options.label: Straight up
options.feedback: A young head is tilted, not level. It is aimed at where the sun will be.

options.label: West
options.feedback: That is where it finished the previous evening. It turns back overnight.

options.label: Whichever way the wind blows
options.feedback: The turning is slow, steady and the same every day. Wind has nothing to do with it.

options.label: East
options.feedback: It spent the night swinging back to meet the sunrise.

items.ok_line: It turned back in the dark to be ready.
items.ko_line: The head ends the day facing west. Something must happen before dawn.
items.exp_text: Through the day the east side of the stem grows faster than the west, and the head tips slowly across the sky. After sunset the growth reverses: the west side lengthens, and the head swings back through the night. By the time the sun comes up, the sunflower is already facing east and waiting for it.

items.prompt: What happens to a sunflower's tracking once it is fully grown?

options.label: It stops, and settles facing east
options.feedback: The stem stiffens and the head stays pointed at the sunrise.

options.label: It tracks faster than before
options.feedback: The turning slows and then ceases. A woody stem cannot bend any more.

options.label: It settles facing west
options.feedback: It halts on the eastward side of its swing, not the westward one.

options.label: It begins tracking the moon
options.feedback: Moonlight is far too faint to drive growth, and the head has stopped moving by then.

items.ok_line: The last turn it makes is the one it keeps.
items.ko_line: Tracking needs a stem soft enough to bend. Ask what an old stem is like.
items.exp_title: The stem sets, and the aim sticks
items.exp_text: Tracking depends on one side of the stem outgrowing the other, and that only works while the stem is still soft. As the plant matures the stem stiffens and the daily swing gets smaller until it stops. The head is left where the last swing put it, facing east.

items.prompt: What does an east-facing sunflower head gain from the morning sun?

options.label: It stays dry in the rain
options.feedback: Rain comes from any direction. The tilt of a head does little against it.

options.label: It warms early, and insects come to it
options.feedback: A warm flower is worth visiting, and the early visitor does the pollinating.

options.label: It gets more light in total
options.feedback: A head fixed east misses the afternoon entirely. It trades quantity for timing.

options.label: It ripens its seeds faster
options.feedback: Seeds ripen on warmth over weeks, and a west-facing head gets its share of that too.

items.ko_line: Facing east means missing the afternoon. Whatever it gains must be worth that loss.
items.exp_text: Morning sun on an east-facing head warms the flower before the surrounding air has caught up. Insects are cold and slow at that hour and go where the warmth is, so the warm head is visited first and most. Facing east buys early visitors, and early visitors carry the pollen.

items.prompt: Why are leaves arranged in a spiral up a stem rather than in a straight line?

options.label: So each leaf shades the next as little as possible
options.feedback: Turn each new leaf a little and no leaf sits squarely under another.

options.label: So the stem is stronger
options.feedback: Spacing the leaves does spread the load, but a straight line up two sides would balance it just as well.

options.label: So rain reaches the roots
options.feedback: Water finds its way down whatever the arrangement, and many plants channel it deliberately along the leaves.

options.label: So insects cannot climb
options.feedback: Nothing about a spiral stops a climbing insect. Plants that keep insects off do it with hairs, wax or poison.

items.ok_line: Every leaf gets its own patch of sky.
items.ko_line: Stand under the plant and look up through it. What would a straight line of leaves cost?
items.exp_text: Leaves stacked directly above one another would leave the lower ones in permanent shade, working for nothing. Turning each new leaf a fixed fraction of a circle from the one below sends it out over open space instead. Looked at from above, the leaves of many plants form a rosette with almost no overlap — the spiral is what keeps them out of each other's light.

items.prompt: Why do daisies and many other flowers close at night?

options.label: To finish making their nectar
options.feedback: Nectar is made and offered while the flower is open. Closing does not help it.

options.label: Because the cold makes them wilt
options.feedback: A wilting flower droops and does not recover. Closing is reversible, and happens on warm nights too.

options.label: To shelter pollen and warmth from the night
options.feedback: A closed flower keeps its pollen dry and its centre warmer than the open air.

options.label: To hide from birds
options.feedback: Birds are rarely a threat to a flower, and most are asleep at the hour it closes.

items.ok_line: No customers at night, and the goods keep better closed.
items.ko_line: It reopens the next morning, unharmed. So it is doing something on purpose.
items.exp_text: The insects a flower is built for do not fly in the dark, so an open flower at night offers its pollen to nobody while dew soaks it and the cold gets in. Cells at the base of the petals swell and slacken to fold them over, and the flower shuts. Its pollen stays dry and its middle stays warmer than the night air around it.

items.prompt: What does an Arctic poppy do with the cup shape of its flower?

options.label: It gathers rain for the plant to drink
options.feedback: Water sitting in a flower would rot the pollen. The cup faces the sun, not the sky.

options.label: It focuses the sun's warmth on its centre
options.feedback: A curved bowl aimed at the sun is warmer inside than the air outside.

options.label: It traps insects that fall in
options.feedback: The poppy needs its visitors alive and leaving. Trapping them would end the visits.

options.label: It amplifies its scent
options.feedback: Scent spreads on moving air, and a cup would hold it in rather than send it out.

items.ko_line: The flower turns to follow the sun all day. Ask what a curved surface does to sunlight.
items.exp_title: A bowl aimed at the sun
items.exp_text: In the far north the summer sun is weak and the air stays cold, so warmth is worth more to a flower than light. The poppy's cup is curved, and it turns through the day to keep that curve square to the sun, so the light striking the whole bowl is thrown inwards onto the middle. The centre sits several degrees warmer than the air: the seeds ripen faster there, and chilled insects come in to warm themselves.

items.prompt: What happens to a plant that is lit strongly from every side at once?

options.label: It bends towards the strongest side
options.feedback: With every side equal there is no strongest side to choose.

options.label: It stops growing
options.feedback: Plenty of light is what a plant wants. Growth carries on, and faster than in shade.

options.label: It grows straight up
options.feedback: No side is darker, so no side outgrows another, and the stem stays true.

options.label: It grows in a spiral
options.feedback: Stems twine in a spiral for climbing, not in answer to light.

items.ok_line: Nothing to lean towards, so it leans nowhere.
items.ko_line: Bending needs a difference between two sides. Ask what happens when there is none.
items.exp_text: Bending is caused by a difference: the growth substance pools on whichever flank is darker, and that flank lengthens. If every flank is lit the same, the substance spreads evenly and no side gains on another. The stem grows straight up.
